title: Ἥφαιστος
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Poseidon and Athena leave, and Achilles wades on across the flooded plain, borne up by Athena’s strength. The Scamander, still raging, calls his brother the Simois to help him choke Achilles in mud and gravel, and rises against him in a great wave. Hera, afraid for Achilles, sends her son Hephaestus against the river with fire, while she herself will raise the winds. The flames dry the plain, burn the corpses and the river-side trees, and boil the river like a cauldron over a hearth, until the river begs Hephaestus to stop and promises Hera never to defend Troy. At her word Hephaestus puts out the fire. Then the other gods fall to strife among themselves, as Zeus watches from Olympus laughing. Ares springs first at Athena, reproaching her for the wound she once brought upon him through Diomedes.

sentences.t: τὼ μὲν ἄρ’ ὣς εἰπόντε μετ’ ἀθανάτους ἀπεβήτην·
sentences.tr: tō men ar’ hōs eiponte met’ athanatous apebētēn·
sentences.l: The two, then, so having spoken, among the immortals went away;
sentences.i: So the two of them spoke, and went away to join the immortals;
sentences.n: τώ ‘the two’ is Poseidon and Athena, who ended the last part with their promise to Achilles, and the verbs are duals: εἰπόντε ‘having spoken’ (aorist participle) and ἀπεβήτην ‘they went away’ (aorist of ἀποβαίνω). The dual is the Greek number for a pair. μετ’ ἀθανάτους, with the accusative, is ‘to join the immortals’, to go among them. ὥς ‘so’ looks back to what they have just said.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὃ βῆ, μέγα γάρ ῥα θεῶν ὄτρυνεν ἐφετμή,
ἐς πεδίον·
sentences.tr:
autar ho bē, mega gar rha theōn otrynen ephetmē,
es pedion·
sentences.l:
But he went, for greatly the command of the gods urged him on,
to the plain;
sentences.i: But he went to the plain, for the gods’ command urged him strongly on;
sentences.n: ὅ is Achilles. βῆ is the unaugmented aorist of βαίνω ‘go’ (Attic ἔβη), and ὄτρυνεν the unaugmented aorist of ὀτρύνω ‘urge on’; Homer often drops the augment. ἐφετμή (nominative singular) is ‘a command’, here the urging of the two gods; μέγα is an adverb, ‘greatly’, and γάρ gives the reason he moved. The unit ends at the ano teleia after ἐς πεδίον.

sentences.t:
τὸ δὲ πᾶν πλῆθ’ ὕδατος ἐκχυμένοιο,
πολλὰ δὲ τεύχεα καλὰ δαὶ κταμένων αἰζηῶν
πλῶον καὶ νέκυες·
sentences.tr:
to de pan plēth’ hydatos ekchymenoio,
polla de teuchea kala dai ktamenōn aizēōn
plōon kai nekyes·
sentences.i: and the whole plain was full of water poured out, and many pieces of fine armour from young men slain in battle floated there, and corpses;
sentences.n: τὸ δὲ πᾶν ‘and the whole of it’ is the plain. πλῆθ’ is πλῆθε, imperfect of πλήθω ‘be full’, and takes the genitive ὕδατος; ἐκχυμένοιο is the aorist middle participle of ἐκχέω ‘pour out’, passive in sense, so the water is flood that has left its bed. αἰζηοί are ‘vigorous young men’, and δαὶ κταμένων, printed as two words, means ‘slain in battle’ (δαί ‘in battle’, κταμένων from κτείνω ‘slain’); the same word, joined as δαϊκταμένων and rendered ‘cut down’, stands earlier in this book. πλῶον is the uncontracted imperfect of πλώω ‘float’, and its subjects are τεύχεα ‘armour’ and νέκυες ‘corpses’. The unit ends at the ano teleia. Line 301 is metrically irregular as transmitted: the third foot needs a lengthened syllable in καλά, and the fifth foot is a spondee.

sentences.t:
τοῦ δ’ ὑψόσε γούνατ’ ἐπήδα
πρὸς ῥόον ἀΐσσοντος ἀν’ ἰθύν, οὐδέ μιν ἴσχεν
εὐρὺ ῥέων ποταμός· μέγα γὰρ σθένος ἔμβαλ’ Ἀθήνη.
sentences.tr:
tou d’ hypsose gounat’ epēda
pros rhoon aïssontos an’ ithyn, oude min ischen
eury rheōn potamos· mega gar sthenos embal’ Athēnē.
sentences.l:
And of him, high, the knees leapt
as he darted against the stream, straight on, and him did not hold back
the wide-flowing river; for great strength Athena put in.
sentences.i: His knees leapt high as he darted straight on against the stream, and the wide-flowing river could not hold him back; for Athena had put great strength into him.
sentences.n: τοῦ is Achilles, in the genitive as ‘his’ with γούνατ’ ‘knees’, and the participle ἀΐσσοντος ‘darting’ agrees with it, so that the clause says ‘his knees leapt … as he darted’. γούνατ’ ‘knees’ is the subject of ἐπήδα, an imperfect, ‘leapt up’. πρὸς ῥόον ἀν’ ἰθύν is ‘against the stream, straight on’. ἴσχεν is the imperfect of ἴσχω ‘hold back’, and εὐρὺ ῥέων ποταμός ‘the wide-flowing river’ is the Scamander. σθένος is ‘strength’, and ἔμβαλ’ is the aorist ἔμβαλε ‘put into’; the strength is put into Achilles, though the Greek does not say so.

sentences.t:
οὐδὲ Σκάμανδρος ἔληγε τὸ ὃν μένος, ἀλλ’ ἔτι μᾶλλον
χώετο Πηλεΐωνι, κόρυσσε δὲ κῦμα ῥόοιο
ὑψόσ’ ἀειρόμενος, Σιμόεντι δὲ κέκλετ’ ἀΰσας·
sentences.tr:
oude Skamandros elēge to hon menos, all’ eti mallon
chōeto Pēleïōni, korysse de kyma rhooio
hypsos’ aeiromenos, Simoenti de keklet’ aÿsas·
sentences.l:
Nor did Scamander slacken his own might, but still more
he was incensed at the son of Peleus, and he armed the wave of his stream,
rising high, and to the Simois he gave orders, shouting:
sentences.i: But Scamander did not slacken his own might; he was incensed still more at the son of Peleus, and armed the wave of his stream, lifting himself high, and shouted orders to the Simois:
sentences.n: Σκάμανδρος is the river and its god at once, and Ξάνθος in lines 332 and 337 is the same river under a second name. τὸ ὃν μένος is ‘his own might’: ὅς here is the possessive, not the relative, and μένος is ‘might’. ἔληγε is the imperfect of λήγω ‘cease, slacken’; χώετο is the imperfect of χώομαι ‘be incensed’, with the dative Πηλεΐωνι ‘the son of Peleus’. κόρυσσε is from κορύσσω ‘arm’ (κόρυς is a helmet), said here of a wave: the water is armed as a warrior is, and the wave stands up like a crest. The Simois is the other river of the Trojan plain. κέκλετο is from κέλομαι ‘urge, bid’, and ἀΰσας ‘shouting’ is the aorist participle of ἀΰω; what follows is an appeal for help more than an order.

sentences.t:
φίλε κασίγνητε σθένος ἀνέρος ἀμφότεροί περ
σχῶμεν, ἐπεὶ τάχα ἄστυ μέγα Πριάμοιο ἄνακτος
ἐκπέρσει, Τρῶες δὲ κατὰ μόθον οὐ μενέουσιν.
sentences.tr:
phile kasignēte sthenos aneros amphoteroi per
schōmen, epei tacha asty mega Priamoio anaktos
ekpersei, Trōes de kata mothon ou meneousin.
sentences.l:
“Dear brother, the strength of the man let us check,
both of us at least, since soon the great town of lord Priam
he will sack, and the Trojans in the fray will not stand.
sentences.i: “Dear brother, let us two together check the strength of this man, since soon he will sack the great town of lord Priam, and the Trojans will not stand in the fray.
sentences.n: The river speaks to the Simois, and the man he means is Achilles, who is not named. φίλε κασίγνητε is ‘dear brother’. σχῶμεν is the aorist subjunctive of ἔχω in the sense ‘let us hold back, check’, and ἀμφότεροί περ is ‘both of us at least’. ἄστυ μέγα Πριάμοιο ἄνακτος is ‘the great town of lord Priam’. ἐκπέρσει is the future of ἐκπέρθω ‘sack’, and κατὰ μόθον is ‘in the fray’, μόθος being the close fight. μενέουσιν is the future of μένω ‘stand one’s ground’. Line 308 is metrically irregular as transmitted: φίλε needs its first syllable lengthened, and the feet do not come out regularly from κασίγνητε on.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἐπάμυνε τάχιστα, καὶ ἐμπίπληθι ῥέεθρα
ὕδατος ἐκ πηγέων, πάντας δ’ ὀρόθυνον ἐναύλους,
ἵστη δὲ μέγα κῦμα, πολὺν δ’ ὀρυμαγδὸν ὄρινε
φιτρῶν καὶ λάων,
sentences.tr:
all’ epamyne tachista, kai empiplēthi rheethra
hydatos ek pēgeōn, pantas d’ orothynon enaulous,
histē de mega kyma, polyn d’ orymagdon orine
phitrōn kai laōn,
sentences.l:
But come to the defence very quickly, and fill your streams
with water from the springs, and rouse all the stream-beds,
and raise a great wave, and stir up a great din
of logs and stones,
sentences.i: But come to the defence very quickly: fill your streams with water from the springs, rouse every stream-bed, raise a great wave, and stir up a great din of logs and stones,
sentences.n: ἐπάμυνε is the imperative of ἐπαμύνω ‘come to the defence’, and the four commands that follow say how: ἐμπίπληθι ‘fill’, ὀρόθυνον ‘rouse’, ἵστη ‘set up, raise’ and ὄρινε ‘stir up’. ἐκ πηγέων is ‘from the springs’, with the epic genitive plural in -έων. ἐναύλους are stream-beds, the channels that run in the plain. φιτρῶν καὶ λάων is ‘of logs and stones’, the things the flood will roll along; ὀρυμαγδός is a loud din. The unit ends at the comma because the sentence would otherwise run past four lines.

sentences.t:
ἵνα παύσομεν ἄγριον ἄνδρα
ὃς δὴ νῦν κρατέει, μέμονεν δ’ ὅ γε ἶσα θεοῖσι.
sentences.tr:
hina pausomen agrion andra
hos dē nyn krateei, memonen d’ ho ge isa theoisi.
sentences.l:
so that we may stop the fierce man
who now prevails, and he is set on being equal to gods.
sentences.i: so that we may put a stop to the fierce man, who is now prevailing and is set on being the equal of gods.
sentences.n: ἵνα with παύσομεν gives the purpose, ‘so that we may stop’; παύσομεν is a short-vowel subjunctive of παύω, an old form that looks like a future. ἄγριον ἄνδρα is ‘the fierce man’, still Achilles. κρατέει is the uncontracted κρατεῖ ‘prevails’. μέμονεν is a perfect with present sense, ‘is set on, is eager’, from the root of μένος. ἶσα θεοῖσι is ‘equal to gods’: ἶσα is the neuter plural used as an adverb, with the dative θεοῖσι.

sentences.t:
φημὶ γὰρ οὔτε βίην χραισμησέμεν οὔτέ τι εἶδος
οὔτε τὰ τεύχεα καλά, τά που μάλα νειόθι λίμνης
κείσεθ’ ὑπ’ ἰλύος κεκαλυμμένα·
sentences.tr:
phēmi gar oute biēn chraismēsemen oute ti eidos
oute ta teuchea kala, ta pou mala neiothi limnēs
keiseth’ hyp’ ilyos kekalymmena·
sentences.i: For I say that neither his strength will help him, nor his looks, nor his fine armour, which will lie, I suppose, very deep down in the pool, covered over with mud;
sentences.n: φημί … χραισμησέμεν is ‘I say … will help’, an indirect statement with the future infinitive of χραισμέω ‘help, avail’; the Greek gives no one to be helped, and the English supplies ‘him’. βίη is ‘might’ and εἶδος ‘form’, his fine bearing. τά is the relative ‘which’, with που ‘I suppose’. νειόθι λίμνης is ‘deep in the pool’, with the -θι of place. κείσεθ’ is κείσεται, future of κεῖμαι ‘lie’, and κεκαλυμμένα the perfect passive participle of καλύπτω ‘cover’, with ὑπ’ ἰλύος ‘under mud’. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
κὰδ δέ μιν αὐτὸν
εἰλύσω ψαμάθοισιν ἅλις χέραδος περιχεύας
μυρίον, οὐδέ οἱ ὀστέ’ ἐπιστήσονται Ἀχαιοὶ
ἀλλέξαι· τόσσην οἱ ἄσιν καθύπερθε καλύψω.
sentences.tr:
kad de min auton
eilysō psamathoisin halis cherados pericheuas
myrion, oude hoi oste’ epistēsontai Achaioi
allexai· tossēn hoi asin kathyperthe kalypsō.
sentences.l:
and him himself down
I will wrap in sands, pouring round plenty of gravel,
countless, nor will his bones the Achaeans know how
to gather; so great a slime over him I will cover.
sentences.i: and I will wrap the man himself in sands, pouring round him gravel past counting; the Achaeans will not know how to gather up his bones. I will cover him over with so great a slime.
sentences.n: κὰδ … εἰλύσω is tmesis, κατά standing apart from its verb: ‘wrap up’, future of εἰλύω. ἅλις is ‘in plenty’; χέραδος ‘gravel’ is the object of περιχεύας, the aorist participle of περιχέω ‘pour round’, and μυρίον ‘countless’ agrees with it. οἱ is ‘for him’, so ‘his bones’. ἐπιστήσονται is the future of ἐπίσταμαι ‘know how to’, with the infinitive ἀλλέξαι ‘to gather’; the bones will lie too deep to collect. ἄσιν is from ἄσις, a rare word whose usual sense is ‘slime, mud’. καθύπερθε is ‘over the top’, and καλύψω the future of καλύπτω.

sentences.t:
αὐτοῦ οἱ καὶ σῆμα τετεύξεται, οὐδέ τί μιν χρεὼ
ἔσται τυμβοχόης, ὅτε μιν θάπτωσιν Ἀχαιοί.
sentences.tr:
autou hoi kai sēma teteuxetai, oude ti min chreō
estai tymbochoēs, hote min thaptōsin Achaioi.
sentences.l:
On the spot for him a tomb too will be made, nor will there be any need
of mound-heaping, when the Achaeans bury him.”
sentences.i: His tomb will be made for him right where he lies, and he will have no need of a mound heaped up when the Achaeans bury him.”
sentences.n: αὐτοῦ is the adverb ‘on the spot’. τετεύξεται is the future perfect passive of τεύχω ‘make’, so the tomb ‘will be made’, as a finished fact; the river’s own silt will be the tomb. χρεώ ‘need’ takes the genitive τυμβοχόης, ‘mound-heaping’ (τύμβος ‘mound’ and χέω ‘pour, heap’), so the Achaeans’ funeral mound will not be needed. In ὅτε μιν θάπτωσιν the subjunctive of θάπτω ‘bury’ stands without ἄν, which Homer allows. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ἦ, καὶ ἐπῶρτ’ Ἀχιλῆϊ κυκώμενος ὑψόσε θύων
μορμύρων ἀφρῷ τε καὶ αἵματι καὶ νεκύεσσι.
sentences.tr:
ē, kai epōrt’ Achilēï kykōmenos hypsose thyōn
mormyrōn aphrōi te kai haimati kai nekyessi.
sentences.l:
He spoke, and he rose against Achilles, churning, raging high,
roaring with foam and with blood and with corpses.
sentences.i: So he said, and rose up against Achilles, churning and raging high, roaring with foam and with blood and with corpses.
sentences.n: ἦ, καί closes a speech and starts the action; the speaker was the Scamander, and he is the ‘he’ who now rises. ἐπῶρτ’ is ἐπῶρτο, the aorist middle of ἐπόρνυμι ‘rise against’, with the dative Ἀχιλῆϊ (single λ for the metre). κυκώμενος is ‘churning’, from κυκάω; ὑψόσε is ‘upward, to a height’; θύων is ‘raging’, from θύω ‘rush furiously’; μορμύρων is ‘roaring’. The three datives ἀφρῷ, αἵματι, νεκύεσσι are ‘with foam, with blood, with corpses’, νεκύεσσι being the epic dative plural.

sentences.t:
πορφύρεον δ’ ἄρα κῦμα διιπετέος ποταμοῖο
ἵστατ’ ἀειρόμενον, κατὰ δ’ ᾕρεε Πηλεΐωνα·
sentences.tr:
porphyreon d’ ara kyma diipeteos potamoio
histat’ aeiromenon, kata d’ hēiree Pēleïōna·
sentences.l:
And the surging wave of the Zeus-fallen river
stood up, rising, and was overpowering the son of Peleus;
sentences.i: And the surging wave of the Zeus-fallen river stood up, rising high, and was overpowering the son of Peleus;
sentences.n: πορφύρεον is a colour-word, ‘dark, gleaming’, and said of a wave it means the heaving of the swell, so it is rendered ‘surging’. διιπετέος is the genitive of διιπετής, traditionally ‘fallen from Zeus’, perhaps meaning fed by rain; its sense is not certain. ἵστατ’ is the imperfect middle of ἵστημι, ‘stood up’, and ἀειρόμενον ‘rising’ the participle of ἀείρω. In κατὰ … ᾕρεε, κατά stands apart from its verb (tmesis): καθαιρέω is ‘take down, overpower’, and the imperfect says the overpowering was going on, not finished.

sentences.t:
Ἥρη δὲ μέγ’ ἄϋσε περιδείσασ’ Ἀχιλῆϊ
μή μιν ἀποέρσειε μέγας ποταμὸς βαθυδίνης,
αὐτίκα δ’ Ἥφαιστον προσεφώνεεν ὃν φίλον υἱόν·
sentences.tr:
Hērē de meg’ aÿse perideisas’ Achilēï
mē min apoerseie megas potamos bathydinēs,
autika d’ Hēphaiston prosephōneen hon philon huion·
sentences.l:
And Hera cried out greatly, in fear for Achilles,
lest him the great river, deep-eddying, sweep away,
and at once she addressed Hephaestus, her own dear son:
sentences.i: And Hera cried out aloud, terrified for Achilles, afraid that the great, deep-eddying river might sweep him away; and at once she spoke to Hephaestus, her own dear son:
sentences.n: Hera sees the wave rising against Achilles. ἄϋσε is the aorist of ἀΰω ‘cry out’, and περιδείσασ’ the aorist participle of περιδείδω ‘fear greatly for’, which takes Ἀχιλῆϊ. μή μιν ἀποέρσειε is a clause of fear with the optative, ‘lest it sweep him away’; ἀποέρσειε is a rare compound verb meaning ‘sweep away’, whose root is not certain. μέγας ποταμὸς βαθυδίνης is ‘the great river, deep-eddying’. The last line of the sentence is a whole-line formula: ὅν in ὃν φίλον υἱόν is the possessive ‘her own’, not the relative, and the son is Hephaestus. Line 329 scans only if the first syllable of ἀποέρσειε is lengthened in the second foot, so it is metrically irregular as transmitted.

sentences.t:
ὄρσεο κυλλοπόδιον ἐμὸν τέκος· ἄντα σέθεν γὰρ
Ξάνθον δινήεντα μάχῃ ἠΐσκομεν εἶναι·
sentences.tr:
orseo kyllopodion emon tekos· anta sethen gar
Xanthon dinēenta machēi ēïskomen einai·
sentences.l:
“Rise, bent-footed one, my child; for against you
Xanthus the eddying in fight we reckon to be;
sentences.i: “Rise up, bent-footed one, my child; for we reckon eddying Xanthus to be over against you in the fight;
sentences.n: ὄρσεο is the middle imperative of ὄρνυμι, ‘rise’. κυλλοπόδιον is the vocative of a name for Hephaestus, from κυλλός ‘bent, crooked’ and πούς ‘foot’; he is the lame god. τέκος ‘child’ and ἐμόν ‘my’ show she speaks as his mother. Ξάνθον is the river’s other name. δινήεντα is ‘eddying’. ἄντα σέθεν is ‘over against you’, σέθεν being an epic form of σοῦ, and ἠΐσκομεν εἶναι is ‘we reckon (him) to be’, from ἠΐσκω ‘liken, suppose’; so the gods have set the water against Hephaestus’ fire. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἐπάμυνε τάχιστα, πιφαύσκεο δὲ φλόγα πολλήν.
sentences.tr: all’ epamyne tachista, piphauskeo de phloga pollēn.
sentences.l: But come to the defence very quickly, and make known a great flame.
sentences.i: But come to the defence very quickly, and show a great flame.
sentences.n: The half-line ἀλλ’ ἐπάμυνε τάχιστα is the same in which the river called on the Simois at 311: the two are asked for help in the same words. πιφαύσκεο is the middle imperative of πιφαύσκω ‘make known, show’, so the flame is to be made to appear. φλόγα πολλήν is ‘a great flame’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ Ζεφύροιο καὶ ἀργεστᾶο Νότοιο
εἴσομαι ἐξ ἁλόθεν χαλεπὴν ὄρσουσα θύελλαν,
ἥ κεν ἀπὸ Τρώων κεφαλὰς καὶ τεύχεα κήαι
φλέγμα κακὸν φορέουσα·
sentences.tr:
autar egō Zephyroio kai argestao Notoio
eisomai ex halothen chalepēn orsousa thyellan,
hē ken apo Trōōn kephalas kai teuchea kēai
phlegma kakon phoreousa·
sentences.l:
And I, of the West Wind and of the bright South Wind,
will go, from the sea rousing a harsh storm-blast,
which will burn the heads and the armour off the Trojans,
bearing an evil blaze;
sentences.i: And I will go, and rouse from the sea a harsh storm-blast of the West Wind and the bright South Wind, to burn the heads and the armour off the Trojans, as it bears an evil blaze;
sentences.n: Hera will bring the wind that feeds the fire. The genitives Ζεφύροιο καὶ … Νότοιο belong with θύελλαν ‘a storm-blast of the West Wind and the South Wind’. ἀργεστᾶο is the genitive in -αο of an epithet whose meaning is not known; ‘bright’ is the usual guess. εἴσομαι is ‘I will go’, spelled like ‘I will know’. ἐξ ἁλόθεν is ‘from the sea’, with the -θεν of place-from, and ὄρσουσα is the future participle of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse’, giving the purpose. ἥ κεν … κήαι is ‘which will burn’, with κεν and the aorist subjunctive of καίω; κεφαλάς ‘heads’ stands for the men. φλέγμα is ‘a blaze’. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
σὺ δὲ Ξάνθοιο παρ’ ὄχθας
δένδρεα καῖ’, ἐν δ’ αὐτὸν ἵει πυρί· μὴ δέ σε πάμπαν
μειλιχίοις ἐπέεσσιν ἀποτρεπέτω καὶ ἀρειῇ·
sentences.tr:
sy de Xanthoio par’ ochthas
dendrea kai’, en d’ auton hiei pyri· mē de se pampan
meilichiois epeessin apotrepetō kai areiēi·
sentences.i: and you, burn the trees along the banks of Xanthus, and let fire loose on the river himself; and let him not turn you aside at all, either with gentle words or with threats;
sentences.n: δένδρεα καῖ’ is ‘burn the trees’, καῖ’ being the imperative καῖε. In ἐν … ἵει, ἐν stands apart from its verb (tmesis): ἐνίημι is ‘send into, let loose on’, and πυρί ‘with fire’ is a dative of means. The wording leaves it open whether the fire is let loose upon the river or the god himself is sent in. ἀποτρεπέτω is the third-person imperative, ‘let him not turn you aside’, with μειλιχίοις ἐπέεσσιν ‘with gentle words’ and ἀρειῇ ‘with threat’, ἀρειή being ‘threat’. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
μὴ δὲ πρὶν ἀπόπαυε τεὸν μένος, ἀλλ’ ὁπότ’ ἂν δὴ
φθέγξομ’ ἐγὼν ἰάχουσα, τότε σχεῖν ἀκάματον πῦρ.
sentences.tr:
mē de prin apopaue teon menos, all’ hopot’ an dē
phthenxom’ egōn iachousa, tote schein akamaton pyr.
sentences.l:
And do not stop your might before then, but when indeed
I shall cry out, shouting, then hold back the untiring fire.”
sentences.i: And do not leave off your might until then; but when I cry out aloud, then check the untiring fire.”
sentences.n: μὴ … ἀπόπαυε is a prohibition, ‘do not stop’, with τεὸν μένος ‘your might’; τεόν is the epic form of σόν. ὁπότ’ ἂν … φθέγξομ’ is ὁπότε ἄν with a short-vowel aorist subjunctive, ‘whenever I cry out’, and ἰάχουσα adds ‘shouting’. Hera’s cry is the signal. σχεῖν is the aorist infinitive of ἔχω, used as a command, ‘hold back’, and ἀκάματον πῦρ is ‘the untiring fire’. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφαθ’, Ἥφαιστος δὲ τιτύσκετο θεσπιδαὲς πῦρ.
sentences.tr: hōs ephath’, Hēphaistos de titysketo thespidaes pyr.
sentences.l: So she spoke, and Hephaestus made ready the wondrous-blazing fire.
sentences.i: So she spoke, and Hephaestus made ready his wondrous-blazing fire.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφαθ’ is ‘So she spoke’; ἔφαθ’ is ἔφατο elided, with the τ turned to θ before the rough breathing of Ἥφαιστος. τιτύσκετο is the imperfect of τιτύσκομαι ‘make ready, aim’. θεσπιδαές is ‘wondrous-blazing’: the first part is θεσπι- ‘wondrous, divine’, and the second is usually taken to come from δαίω ‘burn’, but the compound is rare and the second half is not certain.

sentences.t:
πρῶτα μὲν ἐν πεδίῳ πῦρ δαίετο, καῖε δὲ νεκροὺς
πολλούς, οἵ ῥα κατ’ αὐτὸν ἅλις ἔσαν, οὓς κτάν’ Ἀχιλλεύς·
sentences.tr:
prōta men en pediōi pyr daieto, kaie de nekrous
pollous, hoi rha kat’ auton halis esan, hous ktan’ Achilleus·
sentences.l:
First on the plain a fire was kindled, and it burned the corpses,
many, who all about him in plenty were, whom Achilles slew;
sentences.i: First a fire blazed up on the plain and burned the many corpses that lay about him in plenty, the men Achilles had killed;
sentences.n: δαίετο is the imperfect passive of δαίω ‘kindle, blaze’, and καῖε the unaugmented imperfect of καίω ‘burn’. νεκρούς ‘corpses’ takes the relative οἵ, and ἔσαν is ἦσαν ‘were’. αὐτόν is masculine, so it is not the neuter πεδίον ‘plain’; the likeliest reading is Achilles, with the corpses lying round him, as οὓς κτάν’ Ἀχιλλεύς ‘whom Achilles killed’ goes on to say. κτάν’ is κτάνε, the unaugmented aorist of κτείνω (with the augment, ἔκτανε). ἅλις is ‘in plenty’. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t: πᾶν δ’ ἐξηράνθη πεδίον, σχέτο δ’ ἀγλαὸν ὕδωρ.
sentences.tr: pan d’ exēranthē pedion, scheto d’ aglaon hydōr.
sentences.l: And the whole plain was dried up, and the splendid water was held back.
sentences.i: The whole plain was dried out, and the splendid water was held back.
sentences.n: ἐξηράνθη is the aorist passive of ἐξηραίνω ‘dry up’. σχέτο is ἔσχετο, the unaugmented aorist middle of ἔχω, used here with a passive sense, ‘was held back, stopped’. ἀγλαὸν ὕδωρ is ‘the splendid water’.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ ὀπωρινὸς Βορέης νεοαρδέ’ ἀλωὴν
αἶψ’ ἀγξηράνῃ· χαίρει δέ μιν ὅς τις ἐθείρῃ·
sentences.tr:
hōs d’ hot’ opōrinos Boreēs neoarde’ alōēn
aips’ anxēranēi· chairei de min hos tis etheirēi·
sentences.l:
And as when the late-summer North Wind a newly watered orchard
quickly dries up; and he is glad, whoever tends it;
sentences.i: As when the late-summer North Wind quickly dries a newly watered orchard, and whoever tends it is glad;
sentences.n: ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ opens a simile, ‘and as when’. ὀπωρινός is ‘of late summer’, the season of fruit-ripening, and Βορέης is the North Wind. νεοαρδέα is ‘newly watered’ and ἀλωήν ‘orchard’, the planted ground. ἀγξηράνῃ is the aorist subjunctive of ἀναξηραίνω ‘dry up’, in a general comparison. ἐθείρῃ is from ἐθείρω, a rare verb; ‘tend’ is the usual gloss. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἐξηράνθη πεδίον πᾶν, κὰδ δ’ ἄρα νεκροὺς
κῆεν· ὃ δ’ ἐς ποταμὸν τρέψε φλόγα παμφανόωσαν.
sentences.tr:
hōs exēranthē pedion pan, kad d’ ara nekrous
kēen· ho d’ es potamon trepse phloga pamphanoōsan.
sentences.l:
So the whole plain was dried up, and the corpses it burned
down; and he turned his all-shining flame to the river.
sentences.i: So the whole plain was dried out, and the fire burned the corpses down; then Hephaestus turned his all-shining flame on the river.
sentences.n: ὣς answers the simile, and ἐξηράνθη repeats the verb of 345. κὰδ … κῆεν is tmesis, κατακαίω ‘burn down, burn up’; κῆεν is the unaugmented imperfect of καίω. ὅ is Hephaestus, and τρέψε is the aorist of τρέπω ‘turn’. παμφανόωσαν is ‘all-shining’, the uncontracted participle of παμφαίνω.

sentences.t:
καίοντο πτελέαι τε καὶ ἰτέαι ἠδὲ μυρῖκαι,
καίετο δὲ λωτός τε ἰδὲ θρύον ἠδὲ κύπειρον,
τὰ περὶ καλὰ ῥέεθρα ἅλις ποταμοῖο πεφύκει·
sentences.tr:
kaionto pteleai te kai iteai ēde myrikai,
kaieto de lōtos te ide thryon ēde kypeiron,
ta peri kala rheethra halis potamoio pephykei·
sentences.i: The elms burned, and the willows and the tamarisks; the lotus burned, and the rush and the sedge, all that grew in plenty about the river’s fair streams;
sentences.n: These are the plants of a river bank. πτελέαι are elms, ἰτέαι willows, and μυρῖκαι tamarisks; λωτός is a fodder plant, not the lotus-fruit, θρύον is rush and κύπειρον sedge, though the identification of the last three is only the traditional one. καίοντο and καίετο are imperfects of the passive of καίω, ‘burned’. τά is the relative ‘which’, and πεφύκει the pluperfect of φύω ‘grow’. The unit ends at the ano teleia. Line 350 is metrically irregular as transmitted: καί is shortened before ἰτέαι, and the quantities of ἰτέαι and μυρῖκαι have to be forced.

sentences.t:
τείροντ’ ἐγχέλυές τε καὶ ἰχθύες οἳ κατὰ δίνας,
οἳ κατὰ καλὰ ῥέεθρα κυβίστων ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα
πνοιῇ τειρόμενοι πολυμήτιος Ἡφαίστοιο.
sentences.tr:
teiront’ enchelyes te kai ichthyes hoi kata dinas,
hoi kata kala rheethra kybistōn entha kai entha
pnoiēi teiromenoi polymētios Hēphaistoio.
sentences.l:
Were worn down the eels and the fishes, those in the eddies,
those in the fair streams, tumbling here and there,
worn down by the breath of many-wiled Hephaestus.
sentences.i: The eels and the fishes were worn down, those in the eddies and those in the fair streams, tumbling this way and that, worn down by the breath of Hephaestus of many wiles.
sentences.n: ἐγχέλυες τε καὶ ἰχθύες ‘the eels and the fishes’ are the same creatures that fed on the dead Asteropaeus in the last part. τείροντ’ is τείροντο, the imperfect passive of τείρω ‘wear down, distress’, and τειρόμενοι the participle. κυβίστων is the imperfect of κυβιστάω ‘tumble headlong’, and πνοιῇ ‘breath’ is the blast of the flame. πολυμήτιος is the epithet translated ‘of many wiles’ whoever bears it; it is also an epithet of Odysseus.

sentences.t: καίετο δ’ ἲς ποταμοῖο ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζεν·
sentences.tr: kaieto d’ is potamoio epos t’ ephat’ ek t’ onomazen·
sentences.l: And burned the force of the river, and he spoke a word and called him by name:
sentences.i: The river’s force was burning, and he spoke, calling him by name:
sentences.n: καίετο is the imperfect passive of καίω; ἲς is ‘force’, and ἲς ποταμοῖο ‘the force of the river’ is a periphrasis for the river himself, who is the subject of what follows. ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζεν is a formula for speaking to someone by name: ἔφατ’ is ἔφατο elided, the imperfect of φημί, and ἔκ … ὀνόμαζεν (tmesis) is ‘called him by name’.

sentences.t:
Ἥφαιστ’, οὔ τις σοί γε θεῶν δύνατ’ ἀντιφερίζειν,
οὐδ’ ἂν ἐγὼ σοί γ’ ὧδε πυρὶ φλεγέθοντι μαχοίμην.
sentences.tr:
Hēphaist’, ou tis soi ge theōn dynat’ antipherizein,
oud’ an egō soi g’ hōde pyri phlegethonti machoimēn.
sentences.l:
“Hephaestus, no one of the gods is able to vie with you,
nor would I fight you so, you blazing with fire.
sentences.i: “Hephaestus, none of the gods can vie with you, and I would not fight you either, when you blaze so with fire.
sentences.n: Ἥφαιστ’ is the vocative, elided. οὔ τις … δύνατ’ is ‘no one is able’, and ἀντιφερίζειν ‘to vie with, set oneself against’. μαχοίμην with ἄν is a potential optative, ‘I would fight’. πυρὶ φλεγέθοντι is read here as ‘you, blazing with fire’, φλεγέθοντι agreeing with σοί; the words could instead be taken together as ‘with blazing fire’, and the sense is nearly the same. The river is giving in.

sentences.t:
λῆγ’ ἔριδος, Τρῶας δὲ καὶ αὐτίκα δῖος Ἀχιλλεὺς
ἄστεος ἐξελάσειε·
sentences.tr:
lēg’ eridos, Trōas de kai autika dios Achilleus
asteos exelaseie·
sentences.l:
Cease from strife, and the Trojans, even at once, let heavenly Achilles
drive out of the town;
sentences.i: Leave off the strife; as for the Trojans, let heavenly Achilles drive them out of the town at once;
sentences.n: λῆγ’ is the imperative of λήγω ‘cease’, with the genitive ἔριδος ‘from strife’. ἐξελάσειε is an optative used as a wish or a willing concession: ‘let him drive them out’. ἄστεος is the Ionic genitive of ἄστυ ‘town’, the same town the river feared Achilles would sack at 309. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of 360.

sentences.t: τί μοι ἔριδος καὶ ἀρωγῆς;
sentences.tr: ti moi eridos kai arōgēs;
sentences.l: What have I to do with strife and with helping?”
sentences.i: What have I to do with strife, or with giving help?”
sentences.n: τί μοι … ; is ‘what is it to me?’, with no verb: the genitives ἔριδος καὶ ἀρωγῆς name what he has no part in. ἀρωγή is ‘help’, the noun beside ἀρωγοί ‘helpers’ in 371. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: φῆ πυρὶ καιόμενος, ἀνὰ δ’ ἔφλυε καλὰ ῥέεθρα.
sentences.tr: phē pyri kaiomenos, ana d’ ephlye kala rheethra.
sentences.l: He spoke, burning with fire, and up bubbled the fair streams.
sentences.i: He spoke, burning in the fire, and his fair streams bubbled up.
sentences.n: φῆ is the unaugmented form of ἔφη ‘he spoke’, and καιόμενος ‘burning’ is the passive participle of καίω. In ἀνὰ … ἔφλυε, ἀνά stands apart from its verb (tmesis): ἀναφλύω is ‘bubble up, boil over’, and ἔφλυε is the imperfect. καλὰ ῥέεθρα is ‘the fair streams’, the same words as in 354.

sentences.t:
ὡς δὲ λέβης ζεῖ ἔνδον ἐπειγόμενος πυρὶ πολλῷ
κνίσην μελδόμενος ἁπαλοτρεφέος σιάλοιο
πάντοθεν ἀμβολάδην, ὑπὸ δὲ ξύλα κάγκανα κεῖται,
ὣς τοῦ καλὰ ῥέεθρα πυρὶ φλέγετο, ζέε δ’ ὕδωρ·
sentences.tr:
hōs de lebēs zei endon epeigomenos pyri pollōi
knisēn meldomenos hapalotrepheos sialoio
pantothen amboladēn, hypo de xyla kankana keitai,
hōs tou kala rheethra pyri phlegeto, zee d’ hydōr·
sentences.i: As a cauldron seethes within, driven hard by a great fire, melting the fat of a tender-fed pig, bubbling up on every side, with dry wood lying under it, so his fair streams burned with fire, and the water boiled;
sentences.n: A second simile, ὡς δὲ … ὣς, now of boiling in a pot. λέβης is a cauldron, and ζεῖ is ζέω ‘boil’. ἐπειγόμενος ‘pressed, driven hard’ is the cauldron’s state. κνίσην μελδόμενος is ‘melting the fat’; μέλδομαι is ‘melt’ and κνίση the fat, whose smell is what rises. ἁπαλοτρεφέος σιάλοιο is ‘of a pig reared tender’, σίαλος being a fattened pig. ἀμβολάδην is ‘welling up’, and ξύλα κάγκανα ‘dry wood’. φλέγετο is the imperfect passive of φλέγω ‘burn’. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t: οὐδ’ ἔθελε προρέειν, ἀλλ’ ἴσχετο·
sentences.tr: oud’ ethele proreein, all’ ischeto·
sentences.l: nor was he willing to flow forward, but he was held back;
sentences.i: He would not flow on, but was held back;
sentences.n: ἔθελε is the unaugmented imperfect of ἐθέλω ‘be willing’, and its subject is the river. προρέειν is the infinitive of προρρέω ‘flow forward’, and ἴσχετο the imperfect passive of ἴσχω, ‘was held back’. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
τεῖρε δ’ ἀϋτμὴ
Ἡφαίστοιο βίηφι πολύφρονος.
sentences.tr:
teire d’ aÿtmē
Hēphaistoio biēphi polyphronos.
sentences.l:
and wore him down the blast
of Hephaestus, much-minded, with his might.
sentences.i: and the blast of Hephaestus of the many counsels wore him down with his might.
sentences.n: τεῖρε is the unaugmented imperfect of τείρω ‘wear down’, and ἀϋτμή is ‘blast, breath’. βίηφι is the instrumental in -φι, ‘with might’. πολύφρονος agrees with Ἡφαίστοιο; it is translated ‘of the many counsels’ and ‘much-minded’ each time, and it is an epithet Homer also gives to Odysseus.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὅ γ’ Ἥρην
πολλὰ λισσόμενος ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.tr:
autar ho g’ Hērēn
polla lissomenos epea pteroenta prosēuda·
sentences.l:
But he, to Hera
much entreating, winged words spoke:
sentences.i: But he spoke winged words to Hera, entreating her much:
sentences.n: ὅ γ’ is the river, and the speech is to Hera. πολλὰ is the neuter plural used as an adverb, ‘much’, and λισσόμενος ‘entreating’ is from λίσσομαι. ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα is the formula ‘spoke winged words to’; πτερόεντα ‘winged’ is the stock epithet, translated every time.

sentences.t:
Ἥρη τίπτε σὸς υἱὸς ἐμὸν ῥόον ἔχραε κήδειν
ἐξ ἄλλων;
sentences.tr:
Hērē tipte sos huios emon rhoon echrae kēdein
ex allōn;
sentences.l:
“Hera, why has your son my stream set upon, to harm it,
above others?
sentences.i: “Hera, why has your son set upon my stream to harm it, more than the others?
sentences.n: τίπτε is ‘why’. ἔχραε is an aorist of χράω ‘attack, fall upon’, and it takes the infinitive κήδειν ‘to harm’. ἐξ ἄλλων is ‘out of the others’, so ‘more than the rest’. σὸς υἱός is Hephaestus.

sentences.t:
οὐ μέν τοι ἐγὼ τόσον αἴτιός εἰμι
ὅσσον οἱ ἄλλοι πάντες, ὅσοι Τρώεσσιν ἀρωγοί.
sentences.tr:
ou men toi egō toson aitios eimi
hosson hoi alloi pantes, hosoi Trōessin arōgoi.
sentences.l:
I am not so much to blame
as all the others, as many as are helpers to the Trojans.
sentences.i: I am not so much to blame as all the others are, all who are helpers of the Trojans.
sentences.n: οὐ μέν τοι is ‘truly not’, with τοι ‘I tell you’. αἴτιος is ‘to blame’, and τόσον … ὅσσον is ‘so much … as’. ὅσοι Τρώεσσιν ἀρωγοί is ‘as many as are helpers to the Trojans’, with the epic dative plural Τρώεσσιν.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἤτοι μὲν ἐγὼν ἀποπαύσομαι εἰ σὺ κελεύεις,
παυέσθω δὲ καὶ οὗτος·
sentences.tr:
all’ ētoi men egōn apopausomai ei sy keleueis,
pauesthō de kai houtos·
sentences.l:
But I for my part will cease, if you bid,
and let him too stop;
sentences.i: But I for my part will stop, if you bid me; and let him stop as well;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἤτοι μὲν ἐγών is ‘but I, for my part’, and ἀποπαύσομαι the future of ἀποπαύομαι ‘stop’. εἰ σὺ κελεύεις is ‘if you bid’, as in Achilles’ answer to the river earlier (21.223, ὡς σὺ κελεύεις). οὗτος is Hephaestus, and παυέσθω the third-person imperative of παύομαι ‘stop’. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
ἐγὼ δ’ ἐπὶ καὶ τόδ’ ὀμοῦμαι,
μή ποτ’ ἐπὶ Τρώεσσιν ἀλεξήσειν κακὸν ἦμαρ,
μὴ δ’ ὁπότ’ ἂν Τροίη μαλερῷ πυρὶ πᾶσα δάηται
καιομένη, καίωσι δ’ ἀρήϊοι υἷες Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.tr:
egō d’ epi kai tod’ omoumai,
mē pot’ epi Trōessin alexēsein kakon ēmar,
mē d’ hopot’ an Troiē malerōi pyri pasa daētai
kaiomenē, kaiōsi d’ arēïoi huies Achaiōn.
sentences.l:
and I will swear this besides,
that never from the Trojans will I ward off the evil day,
not even when all Troy is burned with devouring fire,
burning, and the warlike sons of the Achaeans burn it.”
sentences.i: and I will swear this oath as well: never to ward off the evil day from the Trojans, not even when all Troy is consumed in devouring fire, and the warlike sons of the Achaeans set it burning.”
sentences.n: ἐπὶ … ὀμοῦμαι is tmesis, ‘swear in addition’, with the future of ὄμνυμι. The oath is in indirect form: μή ποτ’ … ἀλεξήσειν is ‘that never will I ward off’, with the future infinitive of ἀλέξω. κακὸν ἦμαρ is ‘the evil day’. μὴ δ’ ὁπότ’ ἂν … δάηται is ‘not even when … is burned’, with the aorist passive subjunctive of δαίω; μαλερῷ πυρί is ‘with devouring fire’. καιομένη ‘burning’ and καίωσι ‘they burn’ are from καίω, and ἀρήϊοι υἷες Ἀχαιῶν is ‘the warlike sons of the Achaeans’. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ τό γ’ ἄκουσε θεὰ λευκώλενος Ἥρη,
αὐτίκ’ ἄρ’ Ἥφαιστον προσεφώνεεν ὃν φίλον υἱόν·
sentences.tr:
autar epei to g’ akouse thea leukōlenos Hērē,
autik’ ar’ Hēphaiston prosephōneen hon philon huion·
sentences.l:
But when that she heard, the goddess, white-armed Hera,
at once then she addressed Hephaestus, her own dear son:
sentences.i: But when the goddess, white-armed Hera, heard that, at once she spoke to Hephaestus, her own dear son:
sentences.n: τό γ’ is ‘that’, the river’s oath. θεὰ λευκώλενος Ἥρη is ‘the goddess, white-armed Hera’; λευκώλενος is the stock epithet, translated every time. The second line is the formula of 330, with αὐτίκ’ ἄρ’ ‘at once then’; ὅν is again the possessive ‘her own’.

sentences.t:
Ἥφαιστε σχέο τέκνον ἀγακλεές· οὐ γὰρ ἔοικεν
ἀθάνατον θεὸν ὧδε βροτῶν ἕνεκα στυφελίζειν.
sentences.tr:
Hēphaiste scheo teknon agaklees· ou gar eoiken
athanaton theon hōde brotōn heneka styphelizein.
sentences.l:
“Hephaestus, hold back, child, very famous; for it is not fitting
to thrust roughly an immortal god so for the sake of mortals.”
sentences.i: “Hephaestus, hold back, my very famous child; for it is not right to shove an immortal god like this for the sake of mortals.”
sentences.n: σχέο is the aorist imperative middle of ἔχω, ‘hold yourself back’. ἀγακλεές is the vocative of ἀγακλεής ‘very famous’. The ‘immortal god’ is the river, and ἕνεκα βροτῶν ‘for the sake of mortals’ is her argument: gods should not fight so hard over men. στυφελίζειν is ‘to thrust roughly, to shove’. οὐ γὰρ ἔοικεν is ‘for it is not fitting’.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφαθ’, Ἥφαιστος δὲ κατέσβεσε θεσπιδαὲς πῦρ,
ἄψορρον δ’ ἄρα κῦμα κατέσσυτο καλὰ ῥέεθρα.
sentences.tr:
hōs ephath’, Hēphaistos de katesbese thespidaes pyr,
apsorron d’ ara kyma katessyto kala rheethra.
sentences.l:
So she spoke, and Hephaestus quenched the wondrous-blazing fire,
and back again the wave rushed down the fair streams.
sentences.i: So she spoke, and Hephaestus put out the wondrous-blazing fire, and the wave rushed back down its fair streams.
sentences.n: The first line is the line of 342 with a new verb: κατέσβεσε is the aorist of κατασβέννυμι ‘quench’. ἄψορρον is ‘back again’, and κατέσσυτο the aorist of κατασεύομαι ‘rush down’, with the doubled σ of verse; the wave, ending its rise, falls back along καλὰ ῥέεθρα ‘the fair streams’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ Ξάνθοιο δάμη μένος, οἳ μὲν ἔπειτα
παυσάσθην, Ἥρη γὰρ ἐρύκακε χωομένη περ·
sentences.tr:
autar epei Xanthoio damē menos, hoi men epeita
pausasthēn, Hērē gar erykake chōomenē per·
sentences.l:
But when the might of Xanthus was overcome, the two of them then
stopped, for Hera held them back, though incensed;
sentences.i: But when the might of Xanthus was overcome, the two of them stopped, for Hera held them back, incensed though she was;
sentences.n: δάμη is the unaugmented aorist passive of δαμάζω ‘overcome, tame’. οἳ μέν is the pair, the river and Hephaestus, and παυσάσθην is the dual aorist middle of παύω, ‘the two stopped’. ἐρύκακε is a reduplicated aorist of ἐρύκω ‘hold back’, and χωομένη περ ‘although incensed’, with περ giving the concession; Hera is angry still, but she keeps the peace.

sentences.t:
ἐν δ’ ἄλλοισι θεοῖσιν ἔρις πέσε βεβριθυῖα
ἀργαλέη, δίχα δέ σφιν ἐνὶ φρεσὶ θυμὸς ἄητο·
sentences.tr:
en d’ alloisi theoisin eris pese bebrithuia
argaleē, dicha de sphin eni phresi thymos aēto·
sentences.l:
But among the other gods strife fell, weighing heavy,
grievous, and in two ways within their wits their heart was blown;
sentences.i: But among the other gods grievous strife fell, weighing heavily on them, and the heart in them was blown two ways within their wits;
sentences.n: ἔρις ‘strife’ is the subject of πέσε, an unaugmented aorist of πίπτω. βεβριθυῖα is the perfect participle of βρίθω ‘be heavy’, and ἀργαλέη means ‘grievous’. δίχα is ‘in two’. θυμὸς ἄητο: ἄητο is the imperfect passive of ἄημι ‘blow’, so the heart is blown about like something in two winds, divided; ἐνὶ φρεσί ‘in their wits’ names where the division is.

sentences.t:
σὺν δ’ ἔπεσον μεγάλῳ πατάγῳ, βράχε δ’ εὐρεῖα χθών,
ἀμφὶ δὲ σάλπιγξεν μέγας οὐρανός.
sentences.tr:
syn d’ epeson megalōi patagōi, brache d’ eureia chthōn,
amphi de salpinxen megas ouranos.
sentences.l:
And together they fell with a great crash, and the wide earth resounded,
and about, the great heaven sounded like a trumpet.
sentences.i: And they fell together with a great crash, and the wide earth resounded, and all about them great heaven rang like a trumpet.
sentences.n: σὺν … ἔπεσον is tmesis, ‘fell together’, the gods clashing. πατάγῳ is ‘with a crash’, the dative of πάταγος. βράχε is the aorist of βραχεῖν ‘resound’. ἀμφί is ‘all round’. σάλπιγξεν is the aorist of σαλπίζω ‘sound the trumpet’, from σάλπιγξ ‘trumpet’; the great heaven rings as a trumpet does. The unit ends at the full stop in the middle of 388.

sentences.t:
ἄϊε δὲ Ζεὺς
ἥμενος Οὐλύμπῳ· ἐγέλασσε δέ οἱ φίλον ἦτορ
γηθοσύνῃ, ὅθ’ ὁρᾶτο θεοὺς ἔριδι ξυνιόντας.
sentences.tr:
aïe de Zeus
hēmenos Oulympōi· egelasse de hoi philon ētor
gēthosynēi, hoth’ horato theous eridi xyniontas.
sentences.l:
And Zeus heard,
sitting on Olympus; and his dear heart laughed in him
for joy, when he saw the gods meeting in strife.
sentences.i: And Zeus heard it, sitting on Olympus; and his dear heart laughed in him for joy when he saw the gods meeting in strife.
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 388. ἄϊε is the unaugmented imperfect of ἀΐω ‘hear’, and ἥμενος is ‘sitting’. ἐγέλασσε is the aorist of γελάω, with the doubled σ of verse; φίλον ἦτορ is ‘dear heart’, and οἱ ‘in him’ is a dative of the person concerned. γηθοσύνῃ is ‘for joy’. ὅθ’ ὁρᾶτο is ‘when he saw’, the imperfect middle of ὁράω, and ξυνιόντας ‘meeting’ is the participle of ξύνειμι with the old spelling ξυν-; ἔριδι is the dative ‘in strife’.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ οἵ γ’ οὐκέτι δηρὸν ἀφέστασαν· ἦρχε γὰρ Ἄρης
ῥινοτόρος, καὶ πρῶτος Ἀθηναίῃ ἐπόρουσε
χάλκεον ἔγχος ἔχων, καὶ ὀνείδειον φάτο μῦθον·
sentences.tr:
enth’ hoi g’ ouketi dēron aphestasan· ērche gar Arēs
rhinotoros, kai prōtos Athēnaiēi eporouse
chalkeon enchos echōn, kai oneideion phato mython·
sentences.l:
Then they no longer stood apart for long; for Ares began,
the hide-piercing, and first on Athena he sprang,
holding a bronze spear, and he spoke a reproachful word:
sentences.i: Then they did not stand apart much longer; for Ares, the hide-piercer, began it, and was first to spring at Athena, holding a bronze spear, and spoke a word of reproach:
sentences.n: ἀφέστασαν is the pluperfect of ἀφίστημι, with the sense of an imperfect, ‘were standing apart’, the gods having kept back from each other until now. ἦρχε is ‘began’, and ῥινοτόρος is the epithet of Ares: usually taken to mean ‘hide-piercing’ (ῥινός ‘hide’, also a hide shield, and a root meaning ‘pierce’), though the exact sense is not certain. ἐπόρουσε is the aorist of ἐπορούω ‘spring at’, taking the dative Ἀθηναίῃ. χάλκεον ἔγχος is ‘a bronze spear’. ὀνείδειον … μῦθον is ‘a word of reproach’, and φάτο is the unaugmented ἔφατο.

sentences.t:
τίπτ’ αὖτ’ ὦ κυνάμυια θεοὺς ἔριδι ξυνελαύνεις
θάρσος ἄητον ἔχουσα, μέγας δέ σε θυμὸς ἀνῆκεν;
sentences.tr:
tipt’ aut’ ō kynamuia theous eridi xynelauneis
tharsos aēton echousa, megas de se thymos anēken;
sentences.l:
“Why again, O dog-fly, are you driving gods together in strife,
having insatiable boldness, and did a great heart urge you on?
sentences.i: “Why again, you dog-fly, are you driving the gods together into strife, with that insatiable boldness of yours — did your great heart urge you on?
sentences.n: Ares speaks to Athena. τίπτ’ is ‘why’, and αὖτ’ ‘again’. κυνάμυια is ‘dog-fly’ (κύων ‘dog’, μυῖα ‘fly’), an insult, and the vocative. ξυνελαύνεις is ‘you drive together’, from συνελαύνω with the old spelling ξυν-. θάρσος ἄητον is ‘boldness’ with an adjective of uncertain meaning; ‘insatiable’ is one old guess, not a secure sense. μέγας … θυμός is ‘a great heart’, and ἀνῆκεν is the aorist of ἀνίημι ‘urge on’.

sentences.l:
Do you not remember when you urged Tydeus’-son Diomedes on
to wound me, and yourself, taking a spear for all to see,
straight at me thrust, and through my fair flesh tore?
sentences.i: Do you not remember when you urged Diomedes son of Tydeus on to wound me, and yourself took up a spear for all to see, thrust it straight at me, and tore through my fair flesh?
sentences.n: Ares recalls an earlier fight, in which Diomedes wounded him with Athena’s help; he says so himself. μέμνῃ is the second person of the perfect middle of μιμνήσκω, with present sense ‘you remember’. Τυδεΐδην Διομήδε’ is ‘Tydeus’-son Diomedes’. ἀνῆκας is the aorist of ἀνίημι ‘urge on’, with οὐτάμεναι, the epic infinitive of οὐτάω ‘wound’. πανόψιον is of disputed meaning, ‘seen by all’ or ‘all-seeing’; the first is used here. ἑλοῦσα is the aorist participle of αἱρέω, ‘taking’. ἰθὺς ἐμεῦ is ‘straight at me’, and ὦσας the aorist of ὠθέω ‘thrust’. In διὰ … ἔδαψας (tmesis) the verb is the aorist of δάπτω ‘tear’; χρόα is ‘flesh’.

sentences.t: τώ σ’ αὖ νῦν ὀΐω ἀποτισέμεν ὅσσα ἔοργας.
sentences.tr: tō s’ au nyn oïō apotisemen hossa eorgas.
sentences.l: For this reason you in turn now, I think, will pay back all you have done.”
sentences.i: So now, in my turn, I think you will pay for everything you have done.”
sentences.n: τώ ‘therefore’ draws the conclusion. ὀΐω is ‘I think’, and takes the future infinitive ἀποτισέμεν ‘will pay back’, from ἀποτίνω. ὅσσα ἔοργας is ‘all that you have done’, with ἔοργας the perfect of ἔρδω. αὖ ‘in turn’ makes it a repayment. The speech ends here.
